title: Paul of Tarsus and his gospel
excerpt: The gospel of Paul of Tarsus against the Injīl and the men who knew ʿĪsā ibn Maryam: his seven letters, the account in Acts, and the Jerusalem church.

title: Acts against Galatians: Paul of Tarsus in Arabia and Jerusalem
excerpt: How long was Paul of Tarsus in Arabia? Galatians puts Arabia inside the 3 years before his first Jerusalem visit; Acts has no Arabia. Both accounts compared.
body: @consensus

Two accounts survive of the first 15 years of Paul of Tarsus’s life as a follower of Jesus. One is his own, written in anger to the Galatians around 50 to 55 CE and sworn to under oath: “In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie” (Galatians 1:20). The other is Luke’s, written in Acts a generation later by a man who did not know him. They cover the same ground, and at point after point they do not agree.
## The call

Paul of Tarsus says that God “was pleased to reveal his Son in me” (Galatians 1:15-16) and gives no place, no light, no voice and no companions. Acts tells the story 3 times (9:3-9; 22:6-11; 26:12-18), on the road to Damascus, with a light from heaven and a voice. The tellings disagree with one another: in 9:7 the companions hear the voice but see no one; in 22:9 they see the light but do not hear the voice; in 9:7 they stand speechless, in 26:14 they all fall to the ground.

In 9:6 and 22:10 Paul of Tarsus is told to go into the city and await instructions; in 26:16-18 he receives his commission on the spot. All 3 accounts are set side by side in The Damascus road: one vision, three stories at Apostle of Doom.
## After the call

Galatians 1:16-17: “I did not confer with any human being, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were already apostles before me, but I went away at once into Arabia, and afterwards I returned to Damascus.” Acts 9:19-25: he spends “several days” with the disciples in Damascus, preaches in the synagogues, and escapes the city in a basket. There is no Arabia. Paul of Tarsus’s point is that his gospel owed nothing to anyone in Jerusalem; Luke’s is that he was received into the church from the first.
## Paul of Tarsus in Arabia

Galatians gives no length for the stay in Arabia. The one figure is the next: “then after three years I did go up to Jerusalem” (1:18), counted most naturally from the call. Arabia and the return to Damascus together fill those 3 years at most, and ancient inclusive counting can make “three years” little more than 2.

The Arabia of the letter is most likely the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Damascus. Its king, Aretas IV, had the city guarded to seize him, and he escaped through a window in the wall in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:32-33). Paul of Tarsus does not say what he did in Arabia. Some readers take the journey as a retreat towards Sinai, which he places “in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25); others as his first preaching to gentiles, which would explain the king’s hostility.

Acts has no Arabia at all. Between the call and the escape in the basket it has “several days” with the disciples in Damascus and then “some time” (9:19, 23), and it sends him to Jerusalem from there.
## The first visit to Jerusalem

Galatians 1:18-19: “Then after three years I did go up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days; but I did not see any other apostle except James the Lord’s brother.” He adds that he was “still unknown by sight to the churches of Judea” (1:22).

Acts 9:26-30: Barnabas brings him to “the apostles”, he goes in and out among them in Jerusalem, speaks boldly, disputes with the Hellenists, and is sent away when they try to kill him. One account has a private fortnight with 2 men; the other a public ministry among the apostles. Acts 22:17-21 adds a vision in the Temple on this visit that Galatians does not mention.
## The second visit and the council

Galatians 2:1-10: 14 years later he goes up again, by revelation, with Barnabas and Titus, and lays his gospel before the leaders privately. They “added nothing” to him; they agreed that he should go to the gentiles and they to the circumcised, and asked only that he remember the poor.

Acts 15: a public council at which, after debate, James proposes a decree binding gentile believers to abstain from food offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual immorality (15:20, 29). Paul of Tarsus never mentions the decree in any letter. In 1 Corinthians 8-10, writing to a church that would have been bound by it, he treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and knowledge, which he could not have done had he carried the decree to them.

Acts 11:27-30 also records a famine-relief visit to Jerusalem between the first visit and the council, which Galatians, listing his visits under oath to prove how few there were, does not know. The meeting and what followed it are examined in Paul of Tarsus against the disciples at Apostle of Doom.
## Antioch

Galatians 2:11-14: at Antioch, after “certain people came from James”, Cephas withdrew from eating with the gentiles, the other Jews followed, “even Barnabas was led astray”, and Paul of Tarsus opposed Cephas “to his face, because he stood self-condemned”. Acts says nothing of this.
Acts 15:36-40 records instead that Paul of Tarsus and Barnabas parted company over John Mark. Luke’s Paul of Tarsus and Luke’s Peter never quarrel; Luke’s church moves from agreement to agreement.
## Circumcision

Galatians 2:3 says that Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised, and 5:2 says that if you let yourselves be circumcised Christ will be of no benefit to you. Acts 16:3 has Paul of Tarsus circumcise Timothy, whose mother was Jewish, “because of the Jews”. Acts 21:20-26 has him take a Nazirite vow in the Temple to show that he himself keeps the law. Set beside the letters, the Paul of Tarsus of Acts is far more observant than the one who wrote them.
## Which account to prefer

Where Acts and the letters disagree, the letters are preferred. The rule was stated by F. C. Baur in the 1840s and refined by John Knox in the 1950s, and it governs every page about Paul of Tarsus on this website.

Paul of Tarsus writes first-hand, within a few years of the events, to people who were in a position to contradict him, and he swears to the account. Luke writes 30 to 50 years later, from tradition, with a purpose of his own: to show the church united under the apostles and spreading without a break from Jerusalem to Rome.
Acts is used where the letters are silent and corrected where they speak. Why Acts shows no knowledge of the letters is taken up in Why Acts ignores the letters at Apostle of Doom.
## Why it matters here

Read honestly, Acts and the letters show a man who insisted that his gospel came to him by revelation and not from the men who had known Jesus, who kept his distance from them for years, who quarrelled with their leader in public, and whose closest ally left him. They also show a Jerusalem church under James that sent men to Antioch to pull Peter back into line.

The claim that Paul of Tarsus and the apostles preached one gospel in harmony is Luke’s claim. Paul of Tarsus’s own letters tell a different story. See James and the Jerusalem church and the false apostles.
## Questions about Paul of Tarsus in Arabia
? How long was Paul of Tarsus in Arabia?

Galatians does not say. Paul of Tarsus went to Arabia after his call, returned to Damascus, and went up to Jerusalem “after three years” (Galatians 1:17-18). The stay in Arabia was part of those 3 years, so it lasted anything from a few months to about 2 years.
? Why did Paul of Tarsus go to Arabia?

He does not say. His point in Galatians is that he did not go to Jerusalem or consult the apostles, so that his gospel owed them nothing (1:16-17). The king of the Nabataeans, Aretas IV, later tried to seize him at Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32-33), which suggests he had preached in the kingdom.
? Does Acts mention Paul of Tarsus going to Arabia?
No. Acts 9:19-26 takes him from Damascus to Jerusalem with no journey between, and has him received by the apostles there, where Galatians says he saw only Cephas and James (1:18-19).
## Sources
- Hans Dieter Betz, Galatians, Hermeneia.
- Joseph Fitzmyer, The Acts of the Apostles, Anchor Bible.
- John Knox, Chapters in a Life of Paul.
- Ernst Haenchen, The Acts of the Apostles: A Commentary, on Luke’s purpose.

title: Paul of Tarsus against Jesus
excerpt: Paul of Tarsus vs Jesus: the law, salvation, who Jesus is and the meaning of his death, in the words of the 7 letters and of the gospels.
body: @islamic

The position argued on this website is that the teaching of Paul of Tarsus departs, on the matters that count most, from the teaching of Jesus as the gospels record it: on the law, on what a person must do to be saved, on the person of Jesus, and on the meaning of his death. The Christian reply, set out below, is that Paul of Tarsus is a faithful interpreter of Jesus for a new situation.

Both readings are set out here, each from the texts, so that the reader can judge. Claims about Paul of Tarsus rest on his 7 undisputed letters only; see the seven letters. The portraits that result are drawn side by side in Two portraits of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam at Apostle of Doom.
## The law

Matthew 5:17-19: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfil. For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished. Therefore, whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do the same, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” Matthew 23:2-3: do whatever the scribes and Pharisees teach you, for they sit on Moses’ seat. Luke 16:17: it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter in the law to be dropped.

Galatians 2:16: “a person is justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” Galatians 3:13: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” Galatians 5:2-4: “if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you… You who want to be justified by the law have cut yourselves off from Christ.” Romans 10:4: “Christ is the end of the law.” Romans 7:6: “now we are discharged from the law.” These verses are set against Matthew 5:17 one by one in Paul of Tarsus and the Law at Best of Islam, and the doctrine is traced in Seven doctrines: the law and the covenant at Apostle of Doom.
## What must one do?
Mark 10:17-19: a man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus answers, “You know the commandments,” and lists them.

Matthew 19:17: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” Luke 10:25-28: a lawyer asks the same question; Jesus asks what is written in the law, approves the answer (love God, love your neighbour), and says, “Do this, and you will live.” Matthew 7:21: not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom, but the one who does the will of my Father.

Romans 3:28: “a person is justified by faith apart from works prescribed by the law.” Romans 4:5: “to one who without works trusts him who justifies the ungodly, such faith is reckoned as righteousness.” Romans 10:9: “if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”
## Who Jesus is

Mark 10:18: “Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone.” Mark 12:29: the first commandment is “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.” Mark 13:32: of that day no one knows, not even the Son, but only the Father. John 17:3: “this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”
In the synoptic gospels Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, speaks of God as his Father and the disciples’ Father, and never asks to be worshipped.

Philippians 2:6-11: he was “in the form of God” and did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself; therefore God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. 1 Corinthians 8:6: “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” Romans 9:5 may call Christ “God over all”, depending on how the Greek is punctuated. Paul of Tarsus prays to Christ (2 Corinthians 12:8) and calls on his name (1 Corinthians 1:2).
## The death

In the synoptic gospels Jesus announces his death 3 times and says the Son of Man came to give his life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45); the saying is one verse, and its meaning is disputed. He forgives sins before his death and without reference to it (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48), and the father in the parable receives the prodigal son back with no sacrifice at all (Luke 15:20-24). Repentance and mercy are enough.

For Paul of Tarsus the death is the centre: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3); God put him forward “as a sacrifice of atonement by his blood” (Romans 3:25); “while we still were sinners Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8); “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The gospel he preached, he says, he received by revelation and not from any human source (Galatians 1:11-12).
## Where the atoning death came from

Al-Fārūqī traces the idea to the religious world into which Paul of Tarsus carried the message. The mystery cults of Osiris, Adonis, Attis and Mithras, which filled the eastern Mediterranean in the first century, offered a god who took on the burden of the worshipper’s guilt by dying, and who rose; a baptism in water administered by priests called “fathers”; and a sacred meal in which the worshipper partook of the god’s death and resurrection by eating and drinking in his name.

Tertullian, who knew these rites, thought the devil had parodied the Christian sacraments in them; the historian is more likely to read the resemblance the other way. “The crucified Jesus stepped into the place of the immolated god,” al-Fārūqī writes, “and the doctrine was given the emendations necessary for the new religious ideology.”

What Jesus had taught, a transcendent God and a law to be kept, was Semitic; what the gentile churches received from Paul of Tarsus, a divine saviour whose death was a sacrifice and whose body was eaten in a sacrament, was the religion of the cults in a new name. The Qur’an’s refusal of the cross and of the sonship is, on this view, the refusal of that whole inheritance (al-Fārūqī, pp. 16-21). Whether the doctrine came by revelation or by borrowing is argued at length in Revelation or borrowing? The letters of a man at Apostle of Doom.
## The Christian reply

Christian interpreters answer that Jesus fulfilled the law and that Paul of Tarsus speaks against the “works of the law” as boundary markers, circumcision, food and sabbath, that separated Jew from gentile, and leaves the moral law and obedience as such untouched. Scholars of the “new perspective”, E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, argue that first-century Judaism did not teach salvation by earning it, and that Paul of Tarsus’s target was ethnic exclusiveness.

On the person of Jesus, they argue that the gospels’ Son of Man and the “I am” sayings of John imply what Paul of Tarsus states, and that the earliest Christians worshipped Jesus from the beginning (Larry Hurtado). On the death, they argue that Mark 10:45 and the Last Supper words (Mark 14:24) show Jesus himself gave his death a saving meaning. These are serious arguments and they are stated here as their authors make them.
## Where this page stands

The replies explain the distance and leave it standing. Matthew 5:19 blesses those who keep the least commandments, and Galatians 5:4 says those who seek to be justified by the law are cut off from Christ. A man asked how to inherit eternal life was told to keep the commandments; a man asked the same question by Paul of Tarsus would have been told to believe in the risen Lord.

The Qur’an says of ʿĪsā that he came confirming the Torah (3:50; 5:46), that he was a servant who said only what he was commanded, worship God, my Lord and your Lord (5:117), and that he was neither killed nor crucified (4:157). On each of the 4 matters, the Qur’anic portrait stands with the Jesus of Matthew and Mark and against the Christ of Paul of Tarsus. The evidence is above, and the reader is asked to check it.

The source of Paul of Tarsus’s gospel, by his own account, was a revelation to himself; the men who had walked with Jesus did not share it, and the next pages show how they received it. See James and the Jerusalem church.
## Questions about Paul of Tarsus and Jesus
? Did Paul of Tarsus and Jesus teach the same thing?

Not on the law. Jesus in Matthew says not one stroke of the law will pass and whoever relaxes the least commandment will be called least (5:17-19); Paul of Tarsus says Christ is the end of the law and those who seek to be justified by it are cut off from Christ (Romans 10:4; Galatians 5:4). Asked how to gain eternal life, Jesus said keep the commandments (Mark 10:19); Paul of Tarsus says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28).
? Did Paul of Tarsus believe Jesus was God?

His letters place Jesus above every creature and still below God. He was “in the form of God” and God gave him the name above every name (Philippians 2:6-11), yet “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3) and at the end “the Son himself will also be subjected” to God (1 Corinthians 15:28). Whether Romans 9:5 calls Christ “God over all” depends on how the Greek is punctuated.
? Who was Paul of Tarsus to Jesus?

Neither a disciple nor a companion. He persecuted the followers of Jesus (Galatians 1:13), never met Jesus, and after the crucifixion claimed to have seen him in a vision, “as to one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:8).
## Sources
- E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism, and Paul: A Very Short Introduction.
- James D. G. Dunn, The Theology of Paul the Apostle.
- Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity.
- Hyam Maccoby, The Mythmaker: Paul and the Invention of Christianity, for the case against.
- Geza Vermes, The Religion of Jesus the Jew.

- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983), pp. 16-21, on the mystery religions as the source of the sacraments and the dying god.

title: James and the Jerusalem church
excerpt: The brother who led the first community, and what it required of Paul of Tarsus.
body: @consensus

James, called in the New Testament “the brother of the Lord”, led the Jerusalem community of Jesus’s followers from the 40s until his death in 62 CE. He is the most important figure of the first Christian generation about whom the New Testament says least, and what it says comes mostly from Paul of Tarsus, who did not get on with him. His life and standing are treated at length in James, the brother of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam at Apostle of Doom.
## Who he was
Mark 6:3 names 4 brothers of Jesus, James first among them, and sisters. In the gospels the family does not follow him (Mark 3:21, 31-35; John 7:5). After the crucifixion James is suddenly a leader.

Paul of Tarsus says the risen Jesus “appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7), lists him with Cephas and John as the “acknowledged pillars” of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9), and names him, in that list, first. On his first visit to Jerusalem Paul of Tarsus saw no one but Cephas and “James the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19).

In Acts, James presides over the council of chapter 15 and delivers its verdict (15:13-21), receives Paul of Tarsus on his last visit (21:18), and is the man to whom Peter sends word on leaving prison (12:17). Later tradition made him the first bishop of Jerusalem.
## The men from James

Galatians 2:11-13: “when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood self-condemned; for until certain people came from James, he used to eat with the gentiles. But after they came, he drew back and kept himself separate for fear of the circumcision faction. And the other Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led astray.”

Three things stand out. James had authority enough to send envoys to another city and have Peter obey them. His position was that Jewish believers should keep the food laws even at table with gentile believers.
And Paul of Tarsus lost the argument at Antioch: he does not say that Peter or Barnabas came round, and he never mentions Antioch as his base again.
## Acts 21

On Paul of Tarsus’s final visit to Jerusalem, Acts has James and the elders say: “You see, brother, how many thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and they are all zealous for the law. They have been told about you that you teach all the Jews living among the gentiles to forsake Moses, and that you tell them not to circumcise their children or observe the customs. What then is to be done?” (21:20-22). They ask him to pay for the vows of four men and to purify himself in the Temple, “so all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself observe and guard the law” (21:24). Paul of Tarsus complies. The passage, written by an author friendly to him, shows that the Jerusalem church was entirely law-observant 25 years after the crucifixion, that it had heard what Paul of Tarsus taught, and that its leaders required him to demonstrate in public that the report was false.
## The letter of James

The New Testament letter of James, whoever wrote it, preserves the voice of this wing of the movement. “Faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead” (2:17). “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (2:24). “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become accountable for all of it” (2:10).

The letter takes up Paul of Tarsus’s own example, Abraham, and draws the opposite conclusion from it (2:21-23; compare Romans 4:1-3). Martin Luther, who understood the disagreement, called it “an epistle of straw”.
## His death

Josephus, writing about 93 CE, records that in 62 CE, between the death of one Roman governor and the arrival of the next, the high priest Ananus “convened the judges of the Sanhedrin and brought before them a man named James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, and certain others. He accused them of having transgressed the law and delivered them up to be stoned” (Antiquities 20.200). The fair-minded citizens, Josephus adds, protested to the king, and Ananus was deposed. This is the earliest non-Christian reference to Jesus, and it is a reference to his brother, put to death as a Jew by the Jewish authorities.

Hegesippus, a second-century Jewish Christian quoted by Eusebius, says James was called “the Just”, drank no wine, ate no meat, wore linen, prayed in the Temple so long that his knees grew hard as a camel’s, and was thrown from the Temple parapet and clubbed to death (Ecclesiastical History 2.23). The details are legend; the portrait of a strictly observant Jew is consistent with everything else.
## Why it matters here
The question this website asks of the first community is what the men who knew ʿĪsā ibn Maryam believed, as against what Paul of Tarsus, who did not, taught. James is the answer.

The brother of Jesus led the community; he kept the law and expected other Jews who followed Jesus to keep it; he sent men to Antioch to enforce it; his church required Paul of Tarsus to prove he was not teaching Jews to abandon Moses; and the letter under his name denies justification by faith alone in so many words.

If the Injīl was what Jesus taught his own people, the community under his brother is the nearest witness to it that survives, and that community did not preach the gospel of Paul of Tarsus. The Qur’an’s ʿĪsā, who confirmed the Torah (3:50), would have been at home in James’s Jerusalem. See the Ebionites for what became of that community. The witnesses who stood with him are gathered in The first witnesses against Paul of Tarsus at Apostle of Doom.
## Sources
- Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 20.197-203.
- Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.23, for Hegesippus.
- Richard Bauckham, Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church.
- John Painter, Just James: The Brother of Jesus in History and Tradition.
- Bruce Chilton and Jacob Neusner (eds.), The Brother of Jesus: James the Just and His Mission.

title: The Ebionites
excerpt: The early Jewish followers of Jesus who kept the law and rejected Paul of Tarsus.
body: @consensus

The Ebionites were Jewish followers of Jesus who kept the law of Moses, held him to be a man and a prophet, and rejected Paul of Tarsus. They are known from the writings of the church fathers who opposed them, from the second century to the fifth, and from fragments of a gospel they used. No book of theirs survives whole. Their name is from the Hebrew ebyonim, “the poor”, which was also what the Jerusalem community called itself (Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:26).
## What the fathers report

Irenaeus, writing around 180 CE, gives the earliest account: “Those who are called Ebionites agree that the world was made by God; but their opinions with respect to the Lord are similar to those of Cerinthus and Carpocrates. They use the Gospel according to Matthew only, and repudiate the Apostle Paul, maintaining that he was an apostate from the law. As to the prophetical writings, they endeavour to expound them in a somewhat singular manner; they practise circumcision, persevere in the observance of those customs which are enjoined by the law, and are so Judaic in their style of life that they even adore Jerusalem as if it were the house of God” (Against Heresies 1.26.2).

Origen, in the third century, says the name means “poor” and that they are poor in understanding, and distinguishes two kinds, one accepting the virgin birth and one not (Against Celsus 5.61). Eusebius says they held Jesus to be “a plain and common man, who was justified only because of his superior virtue, and who was the fruit of the intercourse of a man with Mary”, that they kept the sabbath and the whole law, and that they rejected all the letters of Paul of Tarsus, “whom they called an apostate from the law” (Ecclesiastical History 3.27). Epiphanius, around 375 CE, devotes a long and hostile chapter to them (Panarion 30) and quotes from their gospel.
## The Gospel of the Ebionites

Epiphanius preserves 7 fragments of a gospel the Ebionites used, which he says was a mutilated Matthew. The fragments show a harmony of the synoptic gospels in Greek, beginning with the baptism rather than the birth, in which John the Baptist eats honey cakes rather than locusts (the group was vegetarian), and in which Jesus says, “I have come to abolish the sacrifices, and if you do not cease from sacrificing, the wrath will not cease from you.” Whatever else it was, it was a gospel without a virgin birth, without Paul of Tarsus, and with a Jesus who kept the law and opposed the Temple cult.
## What is uncertain

Every source is hostile, and the earliest is a century and a half after the crucifixion. Whether the Ebionites descend directly from the Jerusalem church of James, dispersed after the war of 66 to 73 CE, or arose later among Jewish Christians east of the Jordan, is an open question. The fathers themselves disagree about details, Origen’s two kinds of Ebionite being the clearest example, and some of what Epiphanius reports may belong to other groups.

What is not in doubt is that from the second century onwards there were communities of Jewish followers of Jesus who kept the law, held Jesus to be a prophet and not God, and named Paul of Tarsus as the man who had betrayed the law, and that the Great Church counted them heretics. The fathers’ reports are weighed as testimony in The hostile witnesses at Apostle of Doom, and what the Muslim tradition made of him in Paul of Tarsus in the Islamic tradition.
## The Pseudo-Clementines

A body of writings from the third and fourth centuries, the Clementine Homilies and Recognitions, preserves Jewish-Christian traditions in which Peter is the true apostle and his unnamed “enemy” preaches a lawless gospel on the strength of a vision. In the Homilies Peter tells him that one who has seen a vision cannot be sure it was not a demon, and that the truth was taught to the apostles who heard Jesus in person (Homilies 17.13-19). F. C. Baur identified the enemy with Paul of Tarsus in 1831: the vision and the lawless gospel point to him.

The Letter of Peter to James, prefixed to the Homilies, warns that some gentiles have rejected Peter’s lawful preaching “in favour of the lawless and absurd doctrine of the man who is my enemy”. These texts are late and layered, but they show the argument of Galatians 2 still being fought, from the other side, two centuries on.
## Why it matters here

The existence of the Ebionites shows that Paul of Tarsus’s gospel was contested from the beginning by Jewish followers of Jesus who claimed to be keeping what he taught, and that the side which lost the argument lost its books as well. The Ebionite Jesus, a man and a prophet, born of Joseph and Mary according to some of them, who kept the law and called others to it, is nearer in every respect but one to the ʿĪsā of the Qur’an than is the Christ of the creeds; the Qur’an differs from them on the virgin birth, which it affirms (3:47; 19:20-21).

The resemblance was noticed by the church fathers, who called Islam a revival of the Ebionite heresy, and in modern scholarship by Adolf von Harnack. This website claims that the earliest Jewish witnesses to Jesus and the Qur’an agree on what he was, and that Paul of Tarsus is the point at which the gentile church departed from both. It makes no claim of descent. See James and the Jerusalem church and the false apostles.
## Sources
- Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.26.2; Origen, Against Celsus 5.61; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.27; Epiphanius, Panarion 30.
- Oskar Skarsaune and Reidar Hvalvik (eds.), Jewish Believers in Jesus: The Early Centuries.
- Bart Ehrman, Lost Christianities, chapter on the Ebionites, and Lost Scriptures, for the gospel fragments.
- F. Stanley Jones, Pseudoclementina Elchasaiticaque inter Judaeochristiana, on the Pseudo-Clementines.

title: The seven letters
excerpt: Which letters scholars accept as Paul of Tarsus’s own, and why the argument here rests on them alone.
body: @consensus

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry the name of Paul of Tarsus. Not all of them are his. Since the early nineteenth century scholars have sorted them by vocabulary, style, theology and the church situation they presuppose, and the result is a broad agreement that 7 were written by him, 3 are disputed, and 3 were written in his name by others after his death.
## The 3 groups

- Seven are undisputed: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Almost every critical scholar, Christian or otherwise, accepts these as Paul of Tarsus’s own, dictated between about 50 and 60 CE. 1 Thessalonians is probably the earliest surviving Christian document.

- Three are disputed: Ephesians, Colossians and 2 Thessalonians. Colossians and Ephesians share long sentences, a vocabulary and a view of the church as a cosmic body that the 7 do not have; Ephesians reads in places as an expansion of Colossians. 2 Thessalonians corrects the expectation of 1 Thessalonians that the end is near, and warns against forged letters in Paul of Tarsus’s name (2:2), which is itself a sign of the problem.

- Three are widely held to be later: 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus, the Pastoral Letters. About a third of their vocabulary is absent from the other ten letters; they presuppose ordained bishops, elders and deacons, a fixed deposit of doctrine (“guard what has been entrusted”, 1 Timothy 6:20), and a settled church of the early second century. They are missing from the earliest list of Paul of Tarsus’s letters (Marcion, c. 140) and from the oldest surviving collection (Papyrus 46, c. 200). On that evidence they are usually dated between 100 and 130 CE. The same question, a letter written in an apostle’s name, is put to 2 Peter in Written in Peter’s name at Best of Islam.
## How the sorting is done

The method is the same one used on any ancient author. A writer has habits of vocabulary and sentence structure that are hard to fake across a whole letter. He answers the questions of his own day. He does not contradict himself on matters he cares about.

Measured so, the 7 form a consistent body: short clauses, rhetorical questions, abrupt turns, an expectation that the Lord will come within the writer’s lifetime (1 Thessalonians 4:15-17; 1 Corinthians 15:51), no church offices beyond local “overseers and servants” (Philippians 1:1), and women named as co-workers, deacons and an apostle (Romans 16:1-7).

The Pastorals forbid women to teach (1 Timothy 2:12), lay down qualifications for bishops (1 Timothy 3:1-7), and treat the faith as a body of tradition to be handed on. The difference is one of generation.
## Writing in another’s name

Writing under the name of a revered teacher was common in antiquity and was also condemned in antiquity as forgery when it was detected; the author of 2 Thessalonians condemns it. The church of the second century rejected the Acts of Paul and 3 Corinthians on exactly these grounds. The historian asks whose voice a text preserves. Ephesians preserves the voice of a disciple of Paul of Tarsus a generation on.
## The rule used on this website

Where this website makes a claim about what Paul of Tarsus himself taught, the claim rests on the 7 undisputed letters and on nothing else. A verse from Ephesians, Colossians or the Pastorals is not used to show what he believed, however convenient it might be. The Pastorals’ instruction that women keep silent, for instance, is not charged to his account.

The reason is plain. An argument about a man’s teaching that leans on letters he did not write can be answered by pointing that out, and the argument here is meant to stand on ground that critical scholarship broadly accepts.

Acts, which is a narrative about Paul of Tarsus written a generation later by someone else, is used as a second source and is corrected by the letters where the two disagree; see Acts against Galatians. How the 13 came to stand in the canon is told in How Paul of Tarsus came to own the New Testament at Apostle of Doom.
## What the seven letters are

They are occasional letters, written to particular churches about particular troubles, and dictated to a secretary (Romans 16:22 names one). They are the earliest Christian writings that survive, older than any gospel by 15 to 40 years. They never quote a saying of Jesus from the gospels at length, mention almost nothing of his life before the night he was handed over (1 Corinthians 11:23), and say openly that their author did not learn his gospel from any man (Galatians 1:11-12). That is the Paul of Tarsus this website examines: the one who speaks in his own letters to people who could have contradicted him.
## Sources
- Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, chapters on the Pauline letters and on pseudonymity.
- Bart Ehrman, Forged: Writing in the Name of God, and Forgery and Counterforgery, on the Pastorals and the deutero-Pauline letters.
- Udo Schnelle, The History and Theology of the New Testament Writings.
- Werner Georg Kümmel, Introduction to the New Testament.

title: The false apostles: was Paul of Tarsus one?
excerpt: Was Paul of Tarsus a false apostle? His own charge against his rivals (2 Corinthians 11:13), the first community’s test for an apostle, and how he meets it.
body: @consensus

In 2 Corinthians 11:13 Paul of Tarsus writes of “false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder! Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.” In 11:5 and 12:11 he calls the same men, with heavy irony, “super-apostles”. They had come to Corinth with letters of recommendation (3:1), they were Hebrews, Israelites and descendants of Abraham (11:22), they preached “another Jesus” and “a different gospel” (11:4), and they had persuaded a church he had founded to doubt him. He never names them.
## Who were they?

The letter gives only one side. The rivals were Jewish Christians, by Paul of Tarsus’s own description. They carried letters of recommendation, which means they were sent by someone. They boasted of visions and revelations, which is why Paul of Tarsus is driven to speak of his own (12:1-7).

F. C. Baur, and in a different form Ernst Käsemann and C. K. Barrett, identify them with emissaries from the Jerusalem church, the same party as the “men from James” of Galatians 2:12 and the “false brothers” of Galatians 2:4, carrying the authority of the pillars against a man whose apostleship they did not recognise. Dieter Georgi sees Hellenistic Jewish missionaries of a different kind, wonder-workers trading on eloquence. The first view explains the letters of recommendation and the appeal to Hebrew descent; the second explains the rhetoric. Either way, the quarrel at Corinth was between Paul of Tarsus and other Jewish followers of Jesus who claimed, as he did, to be apostles.
## An accusation with two edges

Paul of Tarsus’s charge is that his rivals preach a gospel other than his own. But his own gospel, by his account, came to him by a revelation that no one else witnessed (Galatians 1:11-12), and his apostleship rested on having “seen Jesus our Lord” in that revelation (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8).

He admits that his claim to be an apostle was disputed: “If I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you” (1 Corinthians 9:2). In Galatians he curses anyone, even an angel from heaven, who preaches a gospel contrary to his (1:8-9). The men on the other side, who had letters from a church and perhaps from the Lord’s brother, would have said the same of him, and their letters would have said why: that he had not known Jesus, that he taught Jews to abandon the law, and that his authority rested on a vision he alone had seen.

Their letters are lost. His survived, and were made scripture. The claim to have seen the risen Jesus, and the 500 witnesses of 1 Corinthians 15, are examined in Five hundred witnesses and an angel of light at Apostle of Doom.
## The twelve and the one

The gospels record that Jesus chose twelve (Mark 3:14) and sent them out (Mark 6:7). After the death of Judas the eleven filled the place from among men “who have accompanied us throughout the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us”, so that the new man would be “a witness with us to his resurrection” (Acts 1:21-22).

That was the first community’s own definition of an apostle: a man who had been with Jesus from the beginning. Paul of Tarsus met none of the conditions and claimed the title anyway, as “one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:8).

The Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, preserving a Jewish-Christian view, have Peter put the objection in words: can a man who has had a vision for an hour be a better teacher than those who heard the Lord for a year? (Homilies 17.19). The question was asked in the first century and has never been answered except by the authority of the man it was asked about.
## What the gospels say about false prophets

Matthew 7:15-23 has Jesus warn of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing, who prophesy and cast out demons in his name, and to whom he will say, “I never knew you; go away from me, you workers of lawlessness (anomia).” Matthew 24:11, 24 warns that many false prophets will arise and lead many astray with signs and wonders.

The test the gospel gives is fruit, and the fruit it names is doing the will of the Father (7:21), which in Matthew means keeping the commandments (5:19; 19:17). The word anomia, lawlessness, is the word the Ebionites would have used of Paul of Tarsus, and it is the word Matthew’s Jesus uses of the prophets he will reject.

This website claims that the first community had a test for apostles, that the test was fidelity to the law of Moses, and that by that test Paul of Tarsus failed, as James’s church told him to his face (Acts 21:21). It does not claim that Matthew wrote the passage about him.
@islamic

The Islamic reading takes the dispute at Corinth, with the dispute at Antioch and the demand made in Jerusalem, as evidence that the first community was divided over Paul of Tarsus, that the division was about the law and about the source of his authority, and that the side which lost did not leave a record because its books were not preserved. The Qur’an says that the followers of ʿĪsā fell into sects and that God would judge between them (5:14; 19:37; 43:65), and that some who were given the book wrote with their own hands and said it was from God (2:79).

The Qur’an never names Paul of Tarsus, and has no need to. It describes a man who said only what he was commanded, worship God, my Lord and your Lord (5:117), and the men who knew him kept the law and called him a prophet.
The one who did not know him taught otherwise, on the strength of a vision, and called those who disagreed false apostles. The reader has the evidence and may decide which man the word fits.
The full case is at apostleofdoom.org, and the Islamic record of that division is in The early Islamic record at Apostle of Doom.
## Questions about the false apostles
? Was Paul of Tarsus a false apostle?

By the test the first community set, yes. An apostle was a man who had been with Jesus from his baptism to his ascension (Acts 1:21-22), and the Jerusalem church under James held its members to the law of Moses (Acts 21:20-21). Paul of Tarsus met neither condition: he claimed the title on the strength of a vision no one else saw (Galatians 1:11-12; 1 Corinthians 15:8) and taught that the law no longer bound.
? Who were the false apostles in 2 Corinthians 11?

Jewish Christian rivals of Paul of Tarsus who came to Corinth with letters of recommendation and preached “another Jesus” (2 Corinthians 3:1; 11:4, 22). F. C. Baur, Ernst Käsemann and C. K. Barrett identify them with envoys of the Jerusalem church; Dieter Georgi reads them as Hellenistic Jewish missionaries.
? What did Jesus say about false prophets?

That they come in sheep’s clothing and are known by their fruit, and that he will say to those who did mighty works in his name, “I never knew you; go away from me, you workers of lawlessness” (Matthew 7:15-23).
## Sources
- Margaret Thrall, The Second Epistle to the Corinthians, International Critical Commentary, volume 2, on chapters 10-13.
- C. K. Barrett, “Paul of Tarsus’s Opponents in II Corinthians”, New Testament Studies 17 (1971).
- Dieter Georgi, The Opponents of Paul in Second Corinthians.
- Pseudo-Clementine Homilies 17, in The Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8.
